extracted.intended_audience: members of scientific societies, editors, and readers interested in scientific criticism and the treatment of contrarian ideas
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for how scientific societies, editors, and critics should treat paradoxical or contrarian scientific claims, satirical reviews, and anecdotal evidence; includes suggestions on editorial vetting, modes of hearing dissent, and empirical testing of extraordinary assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hear contrarian claims under controlled cross‑examination
rubrics_metrics.description: One meeting in the year should be devoted to hearing those who choose to come forward on such conditions: they state their cases, are kept very close to the questions, and the answers are written down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed as a fair method of admitting paradoxers into scientific societies so they can 'state their cases, and stand quiet cross-examination'; author believes this would do much good but suspects few would attend. Example: Captain Woodley was once proposed as a Fellow; the author suggests controlled examination rather than outright exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors must subject humorous/theological critiques to severe inspection
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should not admit theological fun or daring satire without severe inspection by qualified persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Church of England Quarterly Review article is given as a negative example — a craze that should not have been admitted. The warning is that such pieces can confuse satire and review and should be vetted by knowledgeable reviewers before publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer must avoid confusing himself with the satirical persona
rubrics_metrics.description: A reviewer should not confuse himself with the party he is reviewing (i.e., should not become the book or character he aims to criticize).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: the reviewer writing as his own fictional target (Swallow Swift) so often that 'the article becomes the book itself'; concrete advice is to keep identity and critical distance clear in satirical reviews to avoid self-contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthodox theologians should generally avoid using humor in critiques of science
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rule, orthodox theologians should avoid humor because history shows it is difficult to employ in favor of establishment and often leaves the wielder on the side of heterodoxy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If theological argument is not enlivened by bigotry it is seldom worse than narcotic, but theological fun tends to backfire; thus authors and editors in theological journals should be cautious using humor when addressing scientific matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective ridicule requires substantial subject knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: To turn sober demonstration into ridicule successfully requires knowledge deep enough to attack the weak points; ignorance prevents effective satirization of technical subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: satire of algebraical diction (e.g., misconceptions about log(-1), square roots of negatives) will fail unless the satirist understands the mathematics. The author urges 'cyclometers' (critics) to acquire knowledge sufficient to attack algebraic weak points rather than merely lampooning surface errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary anecdotes require empirical testing, not mere repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Anecdotal or popular beliefs (e.g., 'new moon on Saturday followed by twenty days of rain in nineteen out of twenty cases') must be subjected to observation and further evidence before being accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Dr. Forster's Saturday‑moon claim: 'Nothing but the Moon can settle the question' — the correct response is to wait for more data and test the hypothesis rather than accept widespread anecdote. Editors and societies should encourage empirical follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: How many coincidences establish a law depends on perspective and requires rigorous inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of coincidences deemed sufficient to establish a law is not fixed; it depends on how the mind views the matter and demands careful statistical or evidential reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's paradoxical examples (e.g., acquaintances who later became archbishops) highlight how personal patterns can mislead; critics should demand objective standards and sufficient sample size before inferring laws from coincidences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not accept fabricated or post‑hoc literature without verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors/reviewers should verify the existence and authenticity of works and their titles; sometimes a title is invented after the review or a book is a transparent forgery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an article's title may have been written after the review (malt tax example), or a 'book' may be a forgery; editorial practice requires checking provenance and not publishing unverified sensational claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain clarity between critique and parody to avoid self‑defeating satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire that confuses its own voice with the target undermines criticism and risks endorsing the very folly it seeks to lampoon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative example: reviewer slips into the character of his imaginary author and ends up producing the same craziness; editors and writers should ensure satirical frames are transparent and the critical intent remains clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors should consult qualified persons before publishing technical ridicule or attacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Before admitting attacks that purport to expose 'charlatans' or to ridicule technical claims, an editor should have the work inspected by qualified experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to both theological and scientific domains: the Church Review episode shows the harm of unqualified publication; qualified inspection prevents embarrassing publications that misidentify or misunderstand technical matters.
